opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really exciting proof of concept, and I also want to be upfront that it's very early and the results are, in absolute terms, not that good yet.

The basic idea is simple. Interpretability has been bottlenecked on human labor. Someone stares at a neuron, looks at the text that activates it, and tries to work out what it's doing. That doesn't scale. GPT-2 alone has hundreds of thousands of neurons, and the models we actually care about are vastly bigger. So the question we asked was: can we get a language model to do that work for us? We have GPT-4 look at the activations of a neuron in GPT-2 and write an explanation of what it thinks the neuron is doing. Then, and this is the important part, we have a model simulate the neuron based only on that explanation, and we score how well the simulated activations match the real ones. That gives us an automated way to measure explanation quality, and that's what lets you actually iterate and make progress.

On the promise side, a few things make me optimistic. First, it scales with compute instead of with human hours. Second, we saw that explanations get better as the explainer model gets more capable, so the technique should improve as the underlying models improve. And there's a nice recursive aspect: if you want to align systems smarter than us, you'll need AI help to understand what's going on inside them, and this is a concrete first step in that direction.

On the limitations side, there are a lot. Most neurons we explained got pretty low scores. A big part of that is probably that many neurons aren't cleanly about one thing. They're polysemantic, representing several unrelated concepts, so a short natural-language explanation of a single neuron may simply be the wrong unit of analysis. We also only explain correlations: what makes the neuron fire, not what it causally does downstream. And natural language might just not be expressive enough for some of what these networks compute.

There's also a deeper conceptual worry. If you're using a model to explain a model, how much do you trust the explainer? For GPT-2 that's fine, but if you're ultimately trying to catch something like deception in a very capable system, you can't just take another AI's word for it. You'd want ways to verify the explanations that don't bottom out in trusting the AI.

So my overall take: the specific numbers are not where we need them, but the shape of the approach, automating interpretability research and building scalable ways to evaluate it, is the kind of thing I think we need a lot more of.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea of that project was pretty simple. We took GPT-4 and asked it to look at a neuron in a smaller model — GPT-2, in that case — and write a natural-language explanation of what that neuron seems to be doing. You show it a bunch of text snippets where the neuron fires strongly, and it says something like "this neuron activates on references to Marvel movies" or "this fires on the word 'the' after a comma." And then the really important part is you don't just trust that explanation. You have GPT-4 simulate the neuron based on its own explanation — predict where it should fire on new text — and you compare that against the real activations. So you get a score for how good the explanation actually is.

And I think the thing I'm most excited about is that this makes interpretability scalable in a way that it just hasn't been. GPT-2 has something like 300,000 neurons. If you have humans staring at each one, that's not going to happen, and it's definitely not going to happen for the models we actually care about, which are orders of magnitude larger. So the question we were really asking is: can we automate the process? Can we turn interpretability into something where you throw compute at it and you get more interpretability out? Because that's the regime where it starts to be useful for alignment — you want to be able to run this on a model as part of evaluating it, not have a team of researchers spend six months on it.

Now, the limitations are pretty significant, and I want to be honest about that. The first is that the explanations are mostly not very good. We found that only about a thousand neurons out of those 300,000 got explanations that scored above 0.8, which is kind of our threshold for "this is a pretty faithful explanation." Most neurons are polysemantic — they respond to many unrelated things — and a short natural-language sentence just can't capture that. And the explanation quality drops as you go deeper into the network, so the later layers, where the more abstract and arguably more interesting stuff happens, are exactly where the method does worst.

The second limitation is that neurons might just be the wrong unit of analysis. It's quite possible that the right objects to explain aren't individual neurons but some combination — directions in activation space, circuits, whatever. We picked neurons because they're the obvious starting point and the pipeline is clean, but I don't think we should assume that's where the interpretable structure lives.

And the third thing, which is more of a conceptual worry, is that we're explaining a model's behavior on the distribution of text we show it. The explanation might be totally correct on that distribution and tell you nothing about what the neuron does on inputs you didn't think to test. For alignment, that's exactly the case you care about — the weird out-of-distribution situation where the model does something you didn't anticipate.

So the way I'd summarize it is: I don't think this specific technique, as we published it, solves anything. But I think it's a proof of concept for a paradigm that I'm actually pretty optimistic about, which is using AI systems to do the interpretability work on other AI systems, with an evaluation loop that lets you measure whether the explanations are real. And then as the explainer models get better — and we saw that larger explainer models produce better explanations — the whole thing should improve. That's kind of the bet. The thing that would really worry me is if it turned out that the ceiling on explanation quality is low for fundamental reasons, like the network just isn't decomposable in any human-understandable way. That's possible. But I don't think we know that yet, and I'd rather find out by trying hard than by assuming it.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that we can use AI to help us understand AI. Interpretability involves a lot of work that’s difficult to scale if a human has to examine every part of a model. If GPT-4 can help generate explanations and test them, then potentially we can investigate much more of a model than we could manually.

But there’s an important distinction between producing a plausible explanation and actually understanding what’s going on. An explanation can sound convincing and still be wrong. So you want to evaluate it against the model’s behaviour: does it predict when a neuron will activate, including on examples you didn’t use to construct the explanation?

Even succeeding at that would only get you part of the way. Understanding individual neurons doesn’t automatically tell you how a model makes decisions, or whether it will behave safely in a new situation. You’d need to understand how the pieces interact and how those interactions produce behaviour.

So I see this as a promising direction for scaling interpretability research, rather than something that already gives us a reliable safety guarantee. The hope is that increasingly capable models can help us do the research, while we keep developing ways to check whether their explanations are actually useful and correct.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing is that we can use AI to help us understand AI. Interpretability currently involves quite a lot of painstaking human work: you look at which inputs activate a neuron, try to work out what those inputs have in common, and come up with an explanation. GPT-4 can help automate parts of that process.

But generating a plausible explanation isn’t the same as showing that the explanation is correct. One thing you can do is test whether the explanation lets you predict the neuron’s activations on new inputs. That gives you a quantitative way to assess it, although it’s still a fairly limited test of understanding.

There are also questions about scale. Understanding individual neurons in a smaller model is a useful starting point, but it doesn’t mean we understand how a much more capable model makes decisions. A lot of the interesting computation might be spread across many neurons, and the explanations we get might miss important aspects of it.

So I see this as a promising direction for scaling up interpretability research, rather than something that already solves the problem. The hope is that we can make the tools increasingly useful while also getting much better at checking whether their explanations are actually faithful.
